name: test_upload_retries_on_transient_5xx
docstring:
This test makes sure the uploader retries after a transient 5xx from the
storage backend instead of raising right away. We mock the client to fail
once with a 503 and then succeed, and assert upload() is called twice and
returns normally. Added after INFRA-771 where a single blip failed an entire
nightly batch.
output:
Retries once on a transient 5xx from storage and succeeds, rather
than raising immediately.
why: keeps the guarded behavior, drops the ticket and setup narration

name: test_lock_is_released_even_when_the_callback_raises
docstring:
Verifies the lock is released even if the callback passed to with_lock
raises an exception. Without this the lock would stay held forever and
every subsequent caller would hang, which is exactly the deadlock this
test is guarding against. We patch the lock object and assert release()
is called in a finally-style path.
output:
Guards against the lock staying held if the callback raises --
release() must still run.
why: keeps the hazard the test guards, drops the mechanics

name: test_expired_token_is_rejected_before_the_db_lookup
docstring:
This checks that an expired token is rejected purely from its exp claim,
before the code ever queries the database for the session row. That
ordering matters because a revoked-and-expired token should fail for the
cheaper reason; a change that moved the expiry check after the DB lookup
would still pass functionally but would defeat the point of checking
expiry first, which is to avoid a DB hit on already-dead tokens.
output:
Rejects an expired token from its exp claim before the DB lookup
runs, so a dead token never costs a query.
why: keeps the ordering rationale, drops the restated mechanics

name: test_partial_batch_failure_still_commits_the_successful_rows
docstring:
Confirms that when a batch insert has one bad row among many, the good
rows still get committed rather than the whole batch rolling back. This
matters because the caller reports per-row errors back to the user and
expects the successful rows to already be saved; an all-or-nothing rollback
would silently discard work the user believes succeeded.
output:
Good rows in a batch commit even when one row fails; failure isn't
all-or-nothing.
why: keeps the guarantee under test, trims the justification

name: test_cache_miss_falls_back_to_the_read_replica
docstring:
Tests the fallback path: on a cache miss we must read from the replica
and not the primary, because this query pattern runs at high volume and
hitting primary on every miss would overload it. The mock asserts the
primary connection is never touched.
output:
On a cache miss, reads must come from the replica, never the
primary.
why: keeps the hazard (primary overload), drops the incidental detail

name: test_the_converting_arm_reports_the_original_fault
docstring:
The frames the route arm leaves to the service must actually be printed
there.

bulk_close_orders turns a write failure into ValidationError, so the
route receives a rejection type for what is really a fault. Recording it
without frames at the route is only sound while the converting arm itself
reports the original fault with a traceback -- if that arm stopped
reporting it, the route's one-line rejection would become the only record
of a database error, with no stack trace anywhere.
output:
Only sound because the converting arm itself logs the original fault
with a traceback -- otherwise the route's line is the only record of it.
why: keeps the cross-function reporting contract these assertions guard; adapted from bad_test_example.py

docstring:
A rejected bulk-close should show up as a 400 with the service's reason, not
as a traceback in the application logs.

bulk_close_orders raises ValidationError for the ordinary refusal cases --
account not found, unpaid invoices, draft orders awaiting review. The route
catches that, replies 400 with the service's message, and logs one INFO
line. These tests exist because an earlier version logged the same
ValidationError at ERROR with exc_info attached, which printed a full
traceback for a request that had already been handled correctly and paged
an on-call engineer for nothing (see INFRA-2091).

We also cover the one case where a genuinely unexpected exception occurs:
that one must still be logged with a traceback, because it is a real fault
and not a refusal. See test_an_unexpected_failure_still_reports_a_traceback
below.

Related: test_form_submit_rejection_noise.py covers the same disposal for
the web form's submission path.
output:
A rejected bulk-close must log at INFO with no traceback -- only a
genuinely unexpected failure gets an ERROR log with one. Mirrors
test_form_submit_rejection_noise.py for the form-submission path.
why: keeps the log-level contract these tests pin, drops the incident story and ticket; adapted from bad_test_example.py

it returns raises DetachedInstanceError instead of lazy-loading, unlike
most of the rest of the codebase where detached access is normal.

is tied to the session it opens, and reading one afterward raises

docstring:
Timestamp helpers.

Use utc_naive_now() for every naive DateTime column. Passing an aware
datetime into a naive column lets the database driver apply an implicit
timezone cast using the DB session's own TimeZone setting, so the stored
value ends up depending on which session wrote it -- a bug that only shows
up as a few hours of drift and is hard to reproduce locally. Stripping
tzinfo after converting to UTC avoids that entirely. This module also
exports get_current_timestamp_with_timezone() for the aware columns; do
not mix the two helpers on the same column.
output:
Use utc_naive_now() for naive DateTime columns: an aware datetime
written to one gets an implicit session-TimeZone cast, so the stored
value silently depends on which session wrote it. Use
get_current_timestamp_with_timezone() for aware columns instead --
never mix the two on one column.
why: keeps the real timezone gotcha and the never-mix rule

docstring:
Webhook delivery layer.

This module exists because the product team decided customer-facing
webhooks should be delivered out of the main request path so a slow
customer endpoint can never slow down our own API. That decision also
drove the choice of a separate queue rather than a thread pool: a thread
pool shares memory with the request workers and a stuck customer server
could exhaust it, whereas a queue isolates the blast radius entirely. We
also considered and rejected server-sent events for the same isolation
reason.
why: architecture/product rationale essay; no contract for a caller

name: ApiKey
docstring:
Represents an API key issued to a tenant.

An ApiKey with no revoked_at is live; one with revoked_at set is dead and
must never authenticate a request again, even if expires_at is still in
the future -- revocation always wins over expiry. Among live keys, the
prefix column is unique globally so a lookup by prefix alone is enough to
find the candidate row before checking the full hash.
output:
Revocation always wins over expiry: a revoked key never
authenticates again even if not yet expired. Among live keys, prefix
is unique globally, so a prefix lookup alone finds the candidate row.
why: keeps the precedence rule and uniqueness scope, both invisible from columns

name: ExportJob
docstring:
An export job tracked from request to completion.

status moves PENDING -> RUNNING -> DONE or FAILED and never backwards; a
worker that observes RUNNING with no heartbeat for over 5 minutes should
treat the job as FAILED rather than resuming it, since the original worker
may still be alive and resuming would double-write the output file.
output:
status only moves forward (PENDING -> RUNNING -> DONE/FAILED). A
worker seeing RUNNING with no heartbeat for 5+ minutes must mark it
FAILED, not resume it -- the original worker may still be alive and
resuming would double-write the output.
why: keeps the state-machine invariant and the resume hazard

name: _check_seat_before_activating
signature: def _check_seat_before_activating(user: User, new_role: str | None) -> str | None:
docstring:
Seat/license check for a role change or a deactivate-to-activate flip.

Call this before mutating user.is_active or user.role on the
session-attached user: the seat count query filters on User.is_active,
and SQLAlchemy's autoflush would otherwise flush the pending state change
and count the very user being reactivated as already active, blocking the
last legitimate seat. Client-portal users and seat-exempt roles are never
gated. Returns an error message when blocked, None when clear.
output:
Call before mutating user.is_active or user.role: autoflush would
otherwise count the user being reactivated as already active and
block the last seat. Returns an error message when blocked, None when
clear.
why: keeps the autoflush hazard and return contract

name: resolve_locale
body_preview: return wanted if wanted in SUPPORTED else "en"
docstring:
Picks the locale bundle to load for a request.

Falls back to 'en' when the requested locale is not in SUPPORTED,
because 'en' is the only bundle guaranteed to ship with every build --
every other locale is loaded lazily from the CDN and may be missing in
offline or CDN-outage mode. Do not change the fallback to the browser's
Accept-Language header without checking bundle availability first.
output:
Falls back to 'en': it's the only bundle guaranteed to ship with
every build, while others load lazily from the CDN and may be missing
offline. Don't switch the fallback without checking bundle
availability.
why: keeps the fallback rationale and the caution against changing it

name: _logs_with_frames
signature: def _logs_with_frames(call: ast.Call, caught_name: str | None) -> bool:
docstring:
Figures out whether a given logging call would actually render stack
frames if it ran.

The presence of exc_info isn't the whole question: the logging module
treats a falsy exc_info as absent, so exception(..., exc_info=None) prints
no traceback even though the keyword is there, while a bare exception(...)
does print one because the method defaults exc_info to True. We walk the
AST node, look at its keywords, and decide based on that.
output:
exc_info's presence isn't the question: logging treats a falsy
value as absent, so exception(..., exc_info=None) prints nothing while
a bare exception(...) prints a traceback (the default is True).
why: keeps the falsy-exc_info gotcha the helper exists to encode; drops the AST narration; adapted from bad_test_example.py

name: _service_rejecting
docstring:
POSTs a bulk-close whose service call raises, yielding the response and
the patched logger.

lookup would 404 first and the arm under test would never run. This

id decoding, the account lookup, and the service call itself, plus the
logger so assertions can inspect what got logged.
output:
POSTs a bulk-close whose service raises, yielding (response,
logger). The route's own gates are stubbed so the ValidationError is
the service's own -- unstubbed, account lookup would 404 first.
why: keeps why the gates are stubbed (real hazard: wrong error fires first); drops the patch inventory; adapted from bad_test_example.py
